currentContext.business: Exicom Tele-Systems designs, manufactures and services power-electronics hardware across two verticals. In EVSE it sells AC slow chargers (mainly residential) and DC fast chargers for commercial establishments, public charging networks, highways and fleets, to automotive OEMs across passenger vehicles and electric buses, charge point operators and fleet aggregators. In Critical Power it sells DC power conversion systems (SMPS/SMR), hybrid power systems and lithium-ion energy storage that back up telecom networks, primarily to telecom operators and tower companies in India, Southeast Asia and Africa, and increasingly into data centres and other mission-critical infrastructure. Integrated capabilities across product design, manufacturing and after-sales service, with global DC fast-charging reach added through Tritium.

EVSE: Harmony Connect RMS (remote monitoring / predictive diagnostics)
Turnkey EV charging services — site surveys, installation, commissioning and upstream power infrastructure
Critical Power: DC power systems / Switched Mode Power Supply (SMPS) and Switched Mode Rectifier (SMR)
Lithium-ion batteries, including 150Ah and 200Ah battery platforms with advanced battery management
Hybrid Power Systems and solar-hybrid solutions
Integrated "site-in-a-box" outdoor infrastructure with thermal management and intelligent controllers
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) for residential and Commercial & Industrial use, with hybrid inverters and Li-ion battery banks

currentContext.expansion: The defining expansion event of FY2025-26 was the Hyderabad manufacturing facility. The Company commissioned the plant during the year specifically to scale production capacity and support growing demand across markets, and states that its operationalisation significantly enhanced production scalability and strengthened the Company's ability to serve growing domestic and international demand for EV charging infrastructure. Manufactured capital now rests on advanced manufacturing facilities at Hyderabad and Gurugram, with automated assembly lines, testing infrastructure and scalable production lines for both EV chargers and power systems. Alongside the plant, the EVSE division scaled through next-generation product platforms (Harmony DC Chargers Gen 2.0, Spin Free 2.0 for AC retail charging) and integrated deployment offerings (Harmony Connect RMS and Exicom One, an integrated charging-site solution designed to accelerate infrastructure deployment). Geographic expansion continued in parallel: market presence was strengthened across Southeast Asia and the Middle East while entry pathways were built into Europe and North America, extending the global expansion step taken in 2024 with the acquisition of Tritium. Stated growth priorities are DC fast charging expansion, integrated solutions growth, global market expansion, software and digital platforms, manufacturing scale-up, OEM and ecosystem partnerships, service and lifecycle revenue, product innovation, energy storage solutions and operational efficiency, backed by investments in manufacturing capacity and global expansion. No rupee capex quantum, project cost, or commissioning-date schedule is disclosed anywhere in this bundle.

risks.risk: Supply chain and import dependence on critical electronic components
risks.note: The Risk & Mitigation table flags dependence on imported critical components, notably semiconductors and power electronics, exposing the Company to shortages, lead-time volatility and geopolitical disruption; the Threats section adds that volatility in availability and pricing of components, metals and raw materials could impact procurement costs and project execution timelines. Mitigation is multi-vendor and alternate-region sourcing, buffer stock, supplier long-term forecasting and progressive localisation.

risks.risk: Competition and pricing pressure in commoditising charging hardware
risks.note: Intense competition from domestic and global players, including established power electronics and automotive component manufacturers, can pressure pricing and margins. The Board's report confirms this is already live: standalone performance was hit by industry-wide pricing pressure in the domestic EV charging segment. Mitigation is differentiation on reliability and service, selective bidding discipline, and a shift toward higher-value software, service and integrated-solution revenue.

The Company states a meaningful share of revenue may come from a limited set of large OEM, telecom and utility customers, making it sensitive to the loss or slowdown of any one account. It is also a two-segment business (Critical Power and EVSE), so a downcycle in either telecom capex or EV adoption flows straight through.

risks.risk: Policy, subsidy and localisation regulation risk
risks.note: The pace of EV adoption and infrastructure deployment depends on government incentives, localisation norms, import regulations and evolving policy frameworks; changes in subsidy structures or delays in policy implementation may affect market growth and investment cycles. Critical Power demand is similarly tied to government programmes such as BharatNet.

risks.risk: Technology obsolescence in a fast-moving charging standard set
risks.note: The Company flags that falling behind in technology can weaken its competitive position and future growth prospects, naming V2G readiness and Plug-and-Charge compatibility as the advances it must keep pace with. Hardware differentiation erodes quickly as high-power DC and software-enabled platforms become the baseline.

risks.risk: Overseas scale-up and Tritium integration weighing on consolidated profitability
risks.note: The Board's report states consolidated performance continued to be impacted by investments towards scaling international EV charging operations through Tritium and other overseas initiatives, with continued spend on product development, customer acquisition and operational restructuring. Consolidated results remain materially weaker than standalone.

risks.risk: Project execution timing and order deferment
risks.note: Standalone FY2025-26 performance was impacted by deferment of execution timelines under certain telecom and infrastructure projects and by slower momentum in the EV ecosystem early in the year. The Company also flags strategic risk — that poorly executed long-term plans mean missed growth and expansion opportunities — mitigated through defined project governance and approval processes.

Sudden changes in input costs or foreign exchange rates can pressure profitability, a live exposure given imported components and a growing export/international footprint. Mitigation is hedging tools, contractual flexibility and increased local sourcing.

themes.title: Auto components & EV-driveline localization
themes.need: Premiumization, content-per-vehicle rise and EV/hybrid transition pull a deep auto-ancillary chain - MOTHERSON/SONACOMS/BOSCHLTD/SCHAEFFLER/SKFINDIA/UNOMINDA-tier on driveline, bearings, wiring (MSUMI) and EV systems; OLAELEC/ATHERENERG/OLECTRA on EV OEMs (OLAELEC targeting cell-to-pack 10-15% cost edge); SUNDRMFAST/ENDURANCE/CRAFTSMAN/BHARATFORG on forgings/machining. Q1FY27 showed contracted pricing finally landing for Tier-2s: SSWL earned EBITDA/wheel of Rs 314 against Rs 262 YoY, which management attributed mostly to two years of OEM input-price increases finally landing (1-5%, more pending) rather than mix, with all plants above 95% utilisation and knuckles at 100%; KROSS delivered a 12.23% EBITDA margin (+63bps) BEFORE two retrospective pass-throughs land (steel settled ~15 July, the CV conversion-cost settlement still pending), making Q1 a floor rather than a peak.
themes.driver: GST 2.0 demand pull; retrospective OEM price pass-throughs still to land (KROSS CV conversion cost); EV cell/Gigafactory ramps (OLAELEC 6GWh by June); export + new-platform content wins.

one_liner.body: Exicom is one of the leading providers of EV charging and critical power solutions, with capabilities spanning the entire EV charger value chain and more than 2,15,000 EV chargers sold globally.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Exicom Tele-Systems designs, manufactures and services power-electronics hardware across two verticals. In EVSE it sells AC slow chargers (mainly residential) and DC fast chargers for commercial establishments, public charging networks, highways and fleets, to automotive OEMs across passenger vehicles and electric buses, charge point operators and fleet aggregators. In Critical Power it sells DC power conversion systems (SMPS/SMR), hybrid power systems and lithium-ion energy storage that back up telecom networks, primarily to telecom operators and tower companies in India, Southeast Asia and Africa, and increasingly into data centres and other mission-critical infrastructure. Integrated capabilities across product design, manufacturing and after-sales service, with global DC fast-charging reach added through Tritium.

group_structure.title: Group structure (profile)

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body: Critical Power: ₹98cr revenue (standalone), down due to Bharat Net/delays; 70% market share in rural telecom battery upgrades; 30% revenue from Africa/SE Asia; EV Chargers: ₹53cr standalone (61% QoQ growth), 50% AC/50% DC mix; Harmony Gen 2 adopted by 6 of top 10 customers; Tritium: $8M Q1 bookings, TRI-FLEX pipeline building, lifetime warranty on power modules launched

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:

order_book.title: Order book & pipeline
order_book.body: ₹1,500+ crores total (₹1,200+ crores hardware), including large lithium-ion battery upgrades, Middle East/Africa exports, and EV charger framework agreements in Southeast Asia

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: Revenue growth: 50% YoY standalone; EBITDA: 2.5x improvement; Order inflow: Sustained by ₹1,500cr backlog; Capex/commissioning: Hyderabad plant SOP in Oct 2025, full ramp-up by Q4FY26

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: Global EV charging framework with Southeast Asia clean energy player; entry into electric trucking segment; DC microgrid-integrated charging solutions under development; potential Tritium product localization in India

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- EV charging demand is shifting from availability to reliability — the market is moving toward high-power DC architectures with 120 kW+ becoming the baseline for public fast charging, and 'smart' home charging becoming standard for EV owners
- Fleet electrification is no longer a pilot — e-trucks are entering logistics fleets, e-buses crossed 5,200 units in FY26, and OEMs are building out their own fast charging networks
- Telecom operators have announced plans for 120,000+ site upgrades in FY27, with ARPU growth from ₹166 in FY22 to ₹275 in FY26 creating reinvestment capacity; government focus on connecting uncovered villages and borders adds further demand
- Data centres are emerging as a high-growth demand vertical — India's data centre capacity is expected to grow 30% in 2026 alone, with power demand projected to rise 5 to 9x by 2030, needing exactly the intelligent DC power systems, advanced batteries and storage the Company builds
- Global EV charger market estimated at about USD 18.87 billion in CY2025, rising from USD 24.16 billion in CY2026 to around USD 212.18 billion by CY2035, with Asia-Pacific leading in both size and growth
- Global telecom power systems market projected from USD 6.79 billion in CY2025 to about USD 16.27 billion by 2034 at a 10.20% CAGR, driven by 5G deployment, network densification and the anticipated launch of 6G
- Telecom operators are shifting from lead-acid to lithium-ion and toward high-efficiency modular rectifiers, and export customers increasingly favour a pre-engineered 'site-in-a-box' integrating power conversion, storage, solar, thermal management and enclosure
- Telecom power systems are shifting from passive hardware to intelligent, software-managed assets with SNMP telemetry, FOTA updates and predictive maintenance — favouring connected platforms over standalone products
- India GDP growth of about 7.7% in FY2025-26 with the Economic Survey projecting 6.6% in FY2026-27; sectors linked to electrification, clean energy, digital infrastructure, mobility and grid efficiency are placed to benefit from a multi-year investment cycle
- Policy support and localisation are reshaping the industry — state-level charging infrastructure mandates, tax incentives and phased localisation requirements encourage domestic manufacturing while reshaping the competitive landscape
- Headwinds management is watching: hardening tariff regimes between major economies, supply chains being redrawn along geopolitical lines, and currency and commodity swings that can move cost structures quickly
- Standalone FY26 was hit by industry-wide pricing pressure in domestic EV charging, slow early-year EV ecosystem momentum and deferment of certain telecom and infrastructure project timelines, with momentum improving in the latter part of the year on new passenger EV model launches and strong order inflows
- Consolidated performance continued to be impacted by investments in scaling international EV charging through Tritium and other overseas initiatives; the consolidated business turned EBITDA-positive in Q4, a first since the Tritium acquisition
- Tritium backlog heading into FY27 stated at USD 12.6 million, following Q4 revenue of USD 9.7 million (up 157% over the previous quarter), its strongest performance under Exicom's ownership
- DC power systems order worth roughly ₹113 crore won from a major private telco, described as giving good visibility into FY27
- 10 BESS projects commissioned in FY26 with a stated 100 MWh pipeline for FY27
- Executed one of the country's largest fast-charging rollouts, covering 180+ cities and 350+ locations for a leading EV manufacturer, through the Exicom One solution
- Strong order inflows across both EVSE and Critical Power businesses in the latter part of FY2025-26 (Board's report); the value-creation narrative cites a strong order pipeline across EV and Critical Power segments
- Exports doubled to ₹30 crore in the EV charging business, with distributors now active in Southeast Asia and Middle East regions

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: Gross margin improved to 32.7% (standalone) due to richer EV product mix and cost optimization; Harmony Gen 2 delivered higher value with margin expansion; Tritium's high fixed costs drag consolidated margins; Hyderabad plant to reduce per-unit cost by 15-20% at full capacity

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Rights issue ₹260cr allocated: ₹55cr debt repayment, ₹107cr promoter loan conversion, ₹85cr Tritium support, ₹12cr corporate purposes; IPO funds prioritized for Hyderabad plant (₹292cr), working capital, and R&D; no dividend or buyback planned

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The defining expansion event of FY2025-26 was the Hyderabad manufacturing facility. The Company commissioned the plant during the year specifically to scale production capacity and support growing demand across markets, and states that its operationalisation significantly enhanced production scalability and strengthened the Company's ability to serve growing domestic and international demand for EV charging infrastructure. Manufactured capital now rests on advanced manufacturing facilities at Hyderabad and Gurugram, with automated assembly lines, testing infrastructure and scalable production lines for both EV chargers and power systems. Alongside the plant, the EVSE division scaled through next-generation product platforms (Harmony DC Chargers Gen 2.0, Spin Free 2.0 for AC retail charging) and integrated deployment offerings (Harmony Connect RMS and Exicom One, an integrated charging-site solution designed to accelerate infrastructure deployment). Geographic expansion continued in parallel: market presence was strengthened across Southeast Asia and the Middle East while entry pathways were built into Europe and North America, extending the global expansion step taken in 2024 with the acquisition of Tritium. Stated growth priorities are DC fast charging expansion, integrated solutions growth, global market expansion, software and digital platforms, manufacturing scale-up, OEM and ecosystem partnerships, service and lifecycle revenue, product innovation, energy storage solutions and operational efficiency, backed by investments in manufacturing capacity and global expansion. No rupee capex quantum, project cost, or commissioning-date schedule is disclosed anywhere in this bundle.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident and transparent; acknowledged Q1 miss but emphasized strong order book and pipeline; highlighted operational discipline, product innovation, and long-term strategic bets; tone focused on execution and FY26 guidance adherence

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Capabilities spanning the entire EV charger value chain, with integrated product design, manufacturing and after-sales service in-house
- Established domestic EV charging position — the AR's milestone timeline records 60% share in the residential segment and 25% share in the public charging segment as at 2024, and a well-established position among passenger-vehicle OEMs and CPOs
- Two-vertical portfolio (Critical Power 55.7% and EVSE 44.3% of revenue) built on a common power-electronics core, so telecom and EV cycles partly offset each other
- New Hyderabad integrated plant with advanced assembly lines, automated testing, modular production and Industry 4.0-enabled quality gates, giving flexibility across product variants and headroom for scale
- In-house R&D and validation depth — GET hiring into R&D, internal mobility from production into R&D, functional, environmental and safety testing to IEC standards
- Software and service layer on top of hardware — Harmony Connect RMS, EMS platforms, remote monitoring and predictive diagnostics improve uptime and support a shift toward higher-value software, service and integrated-solution revenue rather than price-led competition
- Global footprint extended through Tritium, giving access to advanced DC fast charging technologies and customers across North America, Europe, Southeast Asia and the Middle East
- Certified management systems (ISO 9001, ISO 14001, ISO 45001) across manufacturing, relevant for mission-critical telecom and charging infrastructure customers

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Tritium turnaround slower than expected; geopolitical supply chain delays for rare earth components (minor impact); EV price wars compressing margins; project execution delays due to monsoon/approvals; consolidation risk from smaller competitors

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Exicom is the only Indian EV charger maker designing its own controller (CPU) in-house — a deep tech differentiator; Tritium's lifetime warranty on power modules is a global first, signaling confidence in reliability and a potential industry standard setter

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- FY27 'north stars' set by the MD & CEO: ramp Hyderabad to full utilisation, turn exports into a consistent revenue line, take Tritium to EBITDA breakeven, deepen the service and trust infrastructure that retains customers after the hardware is installed, and grow Critical Power into data centres, industrial infrastructure and commercial energy storage
- Strategic expansion into Battery Energy Storage Systems, leveraging native power-electronics capability — built through partnerships and commercial deployments after 10 projects executed across industries in FY26
- Move from selling boxes to …

challenges.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers
challenges.body:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tritium's prolonged losses and delayed turnaround | Servotech Power Systems | loser | Low | Servotech's growth is in solar/EPC; Exicom's scale, global reach, and integrated manufacturing give it structural advantage in pure-play EV charging |
| Lack of domestic manufacturing scale in EV charging | OEMs (Tata, Mahindra, Hyundai) | beneficiary | High | Exicom's Hyderabad plant and Gen 2 product will become preferred supplier for premium EV makers seeking reliable, high-margin charging infrastructure |

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Tritium] The overseas fast-charging arm remains loss-making at the consolidated level but shows momentum — Q1 bookings of USD 20.8m, described by the CEO as "~2x QoQ", with a stated "second consecutive quarter ~10Mn$ sales".
- [Regulation - Haryana] Building code notified 5-Jun-26 mandates 1:3 charge points per car park for commercial buildings and 1:5 for group housing/RWA, with 100% EV-ready conduits, basement and stilt charging allowed and EV infrastructure exempt from FAR.
- [Regulation - Delhi] Delhi EV Policy 2026 notified 30-Jun-26 with a ₹15,000 Cr four-year outlay, 30,000+ charging points planned, one charging station per OEM dealer, e-3W and e-N1 only from Jan-27, and e-2W subsidy up to ₹30,000.
- [Regulation - PM E-Drive] ₹504 Cr sanctioned in this tranche (~25% of the ₹2,000 Cr charging pool) for 4,874 public chargers, Karnataka largest at 1,243; the deck's own read is that this is "a positive for Industry. Not a very high target market for Exicom".
- [Plant transition] Manufacturing is mid-shift from Gurgaon to Hyderabad, with both plants running in parallel during the transition.
